items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

ctx.x: You mentioned a lot of legendary people in the brass band: Manny Perez. Black Benny, who Louis Armstrong talks about. Jelly Roll [Morton] talks about him. Who were some of the people you saw that had eventually come to have big names, because I imagine you saw a lot of these people before they left New Orleans for good, before the late teens.

Red Allen. Guy Kelly. I didn’t see Jimmie Noone, because he left around 1917, 1918, ’19, ’20, and I wasn’t old enough to realize what I was looking at, knew who these people were. But I knew of them, that they went away. I heard of the Baquet family. I heard of Sidney Bechet. He was a legend. He went when he was around 16 years old. He started traveling with carnival shows and minstrel shows. He was such a phenomenon at that time. People had never heard nobody blow a horn like that. He was a frustrated trumpet…

items.q: And so he knew me. After I met him, he knew me.

ctx.x: I know. He was nice... And so he knew me. After I met him, he knew me. And then, when I went to Chicago... Let me see, this was '32. I went there with Bud Harris. We stayed at a hotel of that a man owned that owned the Grand Terrace.

items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1959-06-30
items.q: Guy Keller played identical like Lewis, the same tone.

ctx.x: And what about the, we can turn it off a second.

The wildest and most exciting time that I saw in the all, back to the wildest trumpet play I saw at that time. Most of the was Lee Collins and all of this, and boy, I heard them all. But the youngster Guy Keller came from Baton Rouge, at the same time Johnny Hander came from across the lake. And I heard them one night in the entertainers' nightclub. And they were real wild. I never heard nobody play kind of like Johnny Hander. And it was surprising that he would play, pick up the horn in the day. And Lewis…
What about banjo players and guitar players?
